analysis.one_liner: Extends the federal milk price support program through 2002 and raises the guaranteed milk price.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Agriculture Committee, dying in a subcommittee with no cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have kept the federal milk price support program alive through 2002, instead of letting it lapse, and raised the government-guaranteed milk price to $10.35 per hundredweight. The government does this by promising to buy dairy products whenever market prices fall below the floor, which props up farm milk prices. It also would have ended a government loan program for milk processors. The bill was introduced in May 1999 and referred to the House Agriculture Committee, which sent it to a subcommittee; it never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Dairy farmers, who would receive higher and more stable milk prices backed by government purchases of surplus cheese, butter, and nonfat dry milk. Processors lose the recourse loan program they could otherwise use.

how_it_helps.text: Extends the milk price support program, scheduled to end after 1999, through 2002, so farmers keep a government-backed price floor for three more years [S2][S3].
Raises the support rate to $10.35 per hundredweight for 2000-2002, guaranteeing farmers a higher minimum price than the market alone would set [S3].
Repeals the recourse loan program for processors, ending a government lending channel while the farmer-facing price floor is expanded [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers, who pay higher milk, cheese, and butter prices under a higher support floor, and taxpayers, who fund government purchases of surplus dairy products whenever market prices fall below the guaranteed rate.

drawbacks.text: A higher milk price support rate raises retail dairy prices, a cost that falls hardest on lower-income households, and forces the government to buy surplus cheese, butter, and milk powder when the market price drops below the floor [S3].
The bill attracted no cosponsors and the Agriculture Committee took no action beyond referral, suggesting even within the dairy-policy debate the proposal had little support [S4][S5].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have delivered real, targeted help to dairy farmers facing the scheduled end of price supports, but the way price supports work means the help is partly paid for by every household at the grocery store and by taxpayers through government purchases of surplus dairy. With no cosponsors and no committee action, the proposal never got a forum where its costs and benefits could be weighed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and then to its Livestock and Horticulture Subcommittee, where it sat until the Congress ended without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Gil Gutknecht introduced the Dairy Revenue Protection Act of 1999 on May 11, 1999 [S1][S5].
The House Agriculture Committee referred it to the Subcommittee on Livestock and Horticulture on May 19, 1999, and requested comment from USDA; no further action was ever taken [S5].
The 106th Congress ended January 3, 2001 with the bill still in subcommittee [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Consumers and taxpayers were spared a higher guaranteed milk price and the associated government purchases, and milk processors kept the recourse loan program the bill would have repealed. Dairy farmers did not get the price floor extension they sought.

for.name: Rep. Gil Gutknecht
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and delivered introductory remarks on June 29, 1999; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Livestock and Horticulture Subcommittee on May 19, 1999 and never reported it out, so it never reached the House floor.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so no partisan pattern is visible in the record.

industries.note: A $10.35 support floor through 2002 would have guaranteed farmers higher milk prices. The cost of that floor shows up as higher retail dairy prices and government purchases of surplus product, so the farmers' gain comes at milk drinkers' expense.

The bill repeals the recourse loan program that lets processors borrow against dairy products from the government. Ending it removes a financing tool, and its repeal pairs with a higher price floor for farmers.
Price supports work through government purchases of surplus dairy when market prices sag below the floor, a direct taxpayer cost that grows as the support rate rises.
